checks.title: Match the question to the evidence
checks.focus: Consistency, modeling capability and phase stability need different evidence.
checks.expected_narration: Three questions sound similar, but require different evidence. First, do the activity data satisfy a thermodynamic relationship? For that question, examine Gibbs-Duhem diagnostics and state the experimental path, assumptions and numerical method. Second, can a chosen model reproduce the observed vapor-liquid equilibrium? Compare calculated and observed pressure and vapor composition, using a specified fit. Third, is a proposed phase state stable? At fixed temperature, pressure and total composition, compare its total Gibbs energy with admissible alternatives. A fitted curve cannot, by itself, answer all three questions. A consistency score does not tell you the amount of each phase. A stability badge does not replace an explanation of the energy comparison. Before reading a result, say which question you are asking. That sentence determines which graph, residual or material balance you should inspect.

checks.title: What Gibbs–Duhem requires
checks.focus: Dimensionless excess Gibbs quantity; product rule; fixed-T/P Gibbs-Duhem; neglected pressure term and variable-T correction.
checks.expected_narration: Start with the excess Gibbs energy per mole, divided by R T. We call this dimensionless quantity g sub E. For a binary liquid, it equals x times the natural logarithm of gamma one, plus one minus x times the natural logarithm of gamma two. Differentiate with respect to x. The product rule gives the logarithm of gamma one over gamma two, plus two derivative terms. At fixed temperature and pressure, Gibbs-Duhem requires those last two terms to add to zero. This is why the derivative of g sub E should equal the logarithm of gamma one over gamma two. Our isothermal teaching example neglects the pressure contribution. For an isobaric data set whose temperature changes, an excess-enthalpy correction is needed. We cannot apply the simplified isothermal relation indiscriminately. The path and assumptions belong beside the result, not just in the calculation settings.

checks.title: D measures net area imbalance
checks.focus: Positive magnitude A-minus; normalized absolute area difference; D below 5%; not every-point percentage error; undefined zero denominator.
checks.expected_narration: For the area test, plot the natural logarithm of gamma one over gamma two against liquid mole fraction x. Call the area above zero A plus. Call the positive magnitude of the area below zero A minus. D is one hundred times the absolute difference of these two magnitudes, divided by their sum. In the isothermal approximation used here, the signed integral over the full composition interval should vanish. Lab three uses the empirical criterion D less than five percent. A small D therefore indicates a small net area imbalance. It is not the percentage error of every measured point. Positive and negative departures can cancel in an integral. Also check composition coverage. If endpoints were extrapolated, the conclusion depends on that extrapolation. If both area magnitudes vanish, the normalized ratio is undefined; do not force a verdict from a zero denominator.

checks.title: Local residual and average score
checks.focus: r = derivative of excess g minus ln(gamma1/gamma2); score 100 mean absolute r; score below 5 dimensionless, not percent; local peak can remain.
checks.expected_narration: The differential diagnostic asks a more local question. Subtract the logarithm of gamma one over gamma two from the derivative of g sub E. The difference is r of x. Exact consistent functions give zero under the stated isothermal approximation. A nonzero numerical residual can come from inconsistent input, differentiation error or noise. Lab three displays one hundred times the mean absolute residual at the interior points. Its teaching threshold is a score below five. This score is dimensionless. Multiplying by one hundred does not make it a percentage error, because there is no relative-error denominator. Notice the distinction between the local curve and its average. A narrow peak can remain even when the average is small. Read both. A pass means that this selected summary met its criterion. It does not prove that every point exactly satisfies Gibbs-Duhem.

checks.title: More points do not remove a defect
checks.focus: 350 K, amplitude .25, 81 points; D 1.956%, score 1.591, r(.35) about -.250; 41 to 161 same synthetic function, not new measurements.
checks.expected_narration: Here is the example from the opening reading. Use the synthetic isothermal data at three hundred and fifty kelvin, a localized defect with amplitude zero point two five, and eighty-one sampling points. D is about one point nine five six percent. The differential score is about one point five nine one. Both summaries pass. Yet the residual near x equal to zero point three five is about negative zero point two five zero. The local departure remains. Changing from forty-one to one hundred and sixty-one points changes D only slightly. These are denser samples of the same synthetic function, not new experimental measurements. More points can improve the numerical approximation and reveal the shape of the defect. Inspect the residual curve before writing your conclusion.

checks.title: What the Van Ness-type fit tests
checks.focus: Consistent NRTL joint P/y fit; relative P error vs absolute y difference; below 1% and 1 percentage point; no certification.
checks.expected_narration: The Van Ness approach examines modeling capability within thermodynamic consistency testing. Our Lab uses a teaching variant. It fits a consistent N R T L activity model jointly to pressure and vapor composition, at the observed temperature and liquid composition. The pressure metric is the mean absolute relative difference, multiplied by one hundred. The vapor-composition metric is the mean absolute mole-fraction difference, also multiplied by one hundred. Their denominators differ. The criteria are pressure error below one percent, and vapor-composition difference below one percentage point. The second is not a relative percentage error in y. Meeting both limits means that this model reproduces these observations under these assumptions. It does not certify each measurement. Missing a limit can reflect the model, property correlations or experimental data. This teaching fit is not the full NIST implementation. Report the method and its assumptions along with the two numbers.

checks.title: Positive curvature is only a local check
checks.focus: Curvature 1/x+1/(1-x)-2A; z=.12 gives positive 3.4697; local not global; negative unstable; zero needs examination.
checks.expected_narration: First check the curvature of the homogeneous curve at the feed. For this model, the second derivative is one over x, plus one over one minus x, minus twice A. At x equal to zero point one two, substitute one over zero point one two, plus one over zero point eight eight, minus six. The result is about positive three point four six nine seven. Positive curvature means that the homogeneous liquid resists infinitesimal composition fluctuations. It does not exclude a lower-energy split into substantially different compositions. To distinguish a globally stable state from a metastable one, we still need an energy comparison with admissible alternatives. Do not stop at the positive sign or at a badge. Write what was tested: local curvature, at the specified feed composition.
